reading.body:
The AFL-CIO appears in 7 AI lobbying filings, and those filings name 19 separate bills, so the federation's AI lobbying is broad rather than focused on one measure.

The pattern is concentration of labor, not of subject. Ten lobbyists are named across the filings, and Riley Ohlson alone appears on all 7. The bills named span both chambers and run from S 1213 to S 4476 and HR 3460 to HR 9363, which is a wide spread of legislative vehicles for a single client in a single reporting period.

For AI specifically, this is the labor side of the governance fight showing up in the disclosure record. The bills named are the ones where AI rules, workforce effects, and employment policy are being written, and the AFL-CIO is registered on them. That matters because compute buildout and data center siting decisions increasingly run through the same committees and the same labor questions about jobs and grid load.

What the data does not say is what the AFL-CIO argued. A filing reports that a firm lobbied on an issue, not the position taken, so nothing here indicates support, opposition, or amendment. The data also does not show spending, outcomes, or whether these bills moved. It covers one client, one registrant, and filings that name AI, and nothing beyond that.

summary: AFL-CIO filed 7 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports on AI held by this site. Its clients, the lobbyists named on those filings and the AI bills they name are below. LDA registrant id 363.
